title: Hilbert's 10th Problem over the Rationals (Open)
description: Surveys the open problem of Hilbert's 10th Problem over the rationals: is there an algorithm deciding whether a polynomial equation has rational solutions? Formalizes the statement, the key reduction from the integer case, and documents known partial results (Poonen, Koenigsmann, Mazur's conjecture).

meta.assumptions: Two axioms: (1) Z Diophantine over Q implies H10/Q undecidable (reduction from MRDP), (2) Mazur's conjecture implies Z not Diophantine over Q (topological argument). The main question H10/Q remains OPEN.

overview.historicalContext:
Hilbert's 10th problem asked (1900) for an algorithm to decide whether a Diophantine equation has integer solutions. After decades of work by Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam, and Julia Robinson, the problem was resolved negatively by Yuri Matiyasevich in 1970: the MRDP theorem shows every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine, making H10/$\mathbb{Z}$ undecidable.

The analogous question over $\mathbb{Q}$ — H10/$\mathbb{Q}$ — remains one of the most important open problems at the intersection of number theory and mathematical logic. The standard approach to proving undecidability would be to show $\mathbb{Z}$ is Diophantine over $\mathbb{Q}$ (i.e., integrality can be detected by a polynomial equation with rational solutions). However, Barry Mazur (1992) conjectured that the topology of rational points on varieties prevents this: the real closure of $V(\mathbb{Q})$ has finitely many connected components for any variety $V$, while $\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$ has infinitely many.

Two landmark partial results narrow the gap: Bjorn Poonen (2009) proved H10 is undecidable over certain subrings of $\mathbb{Q}$ (rings of $S$-integers), and Jochen Koenigsmann (2016) showed $\mathbb{Z}$ is $\forall\exists$-definable in $\mathbb{Q}$ — just one quantifier alternation away from Diophantine (purely existential) definability.
overview.problemStatement: Is there an algorithm that decides, for any polynomial $P(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \mathbb{Z}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$, whether $P = 0$ has a solution in $\mathbb{Q}^n$?
overview.text: Survey of the open problem H10 over Q.
overview.proofStrategy: This is a survey file documenting the open problem rather than proving new results.
keyInsights: H10/Q is OPEN — neither decidable nor undecidable is known
The key reduction: if Z is Diophantine over Q, then H10/Q is undecidable (from MRDP)
Mazur's conjecture (topology of rational points) would block this reduction
Even if Z is not Diophantine over Q, H10/Q could still be undecidable by other mechanisms
Koenigsmann showed Z is ∀∃-definable (not just ∃-definable) in Q — tantalizingly close

sections.title: Open Problem Survey and References
sections.summary: Module documentation presenting H10/Q as an open problem, listing known results (MRDP, Mazur, Poonen, Koenigsmann), and providing references. Establishes that this file is a survey rather than a proof.

sections.title: Rational Diophantine Framework
sections.summary: Defines RatDiophantinePoly (polynomial evaluations over Q), hasRationalSolution (existence of a rational zero), and H10_Rational_Decidable (the Boolean decision procedure). These form the formal statement of H10/Q.

sections.title: Connection to Integer Case via MRDP
sections.summary: Defines IntegersDiophantineOverQ and axiomatizes the key reduction: if Z is Diophantine over Q (integrality detectable by polynomial), then H10/Q is undecidable by MRDP reduction.

sections.title: Mazur's Conjecture as Topological Obstruction
sections.summary: Defines MazurConjecture (closure of rational points has finitely many connected components) and axiomatizes the implication: Mazur's conjecture blocks the standard route to proving H10/Q undecidable.

sections.title: Poonen and Koenigsmann: Partial Decidability Results
sections.summary: Formalizes (as True placeholders) Poonen's 2009 undecidability for S-integer rings and Koenigsmann's 2016 theorem that Z is forall-exists-definable in Q — one quantifier alternation from Diophantine definability.

sections.title: Full Landscape: Logical Dependencies and Open Questions
sections.summary: Status table and logical dependency graph: MRDP (proved) → Z Diophantine/Q → H10/Q undecidable (open chain). Explains why no polynomial is known detecting integrality over Q. Lists axioms and #check commands.

crossReferences.description: Parent: MRDP theorem proving H10/$\mathbb{Z}$ undecidable — the starting point for the reduction approach to H10/$\mathbb{Q}$
Gödel's incompleteness theorems — the foundational undecidability result that underlies MRDP and the computability-theoretic approach to H10
Turing's halting problem — the canonical undecidable problem that MRDP reduces to Diophantine unsolvability
P vs NP — another open problem about computational limits, tangentially related through the decidability hierarchy

conclusion.summary: This file surveys the open problem H10/Q, formalizing the statement and the key logical dependencies. With 2 axioms capturing the main reductions and documented partial results, it provides a formal framework for one of the most important open problems in mathematical logic.
conclusion.implications: Resolution of H10/Q would be a major breakthrough. If undecidable, it would show fundamental limits on rational arithmetic. If decidable, it would require entirely new algorithms beyond classical number theory.
openQuestions: Resolve H10/$\mathbb{Q}$ — the main open problem: is there an algorithm deciding rational solvability of polynomial equations?
Determine if $\mathbb{Z}$ is Diophantine over $\mathbb{Q}$: can integrality be detected by polynomial equations with rational solutions?
Resolve Mazur's conjecture on the topology of rational points: does the real closure of $V(\mathbb{Q})$ always have finitely many connected components?
Extend Poonen's result: find larger subrings of $\mathbb{Q}$ for which H10 is undecidable, approaching $\mathbb{Q}$ itself
Close the quantifier gap between Koenigsmann's $\forall\exists$-definability and Diophantine ($\exists$-only) definability of $\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Q}$
